For an inverse-square bound system, **K = −E** and **U = 2E**.
**Step 1 — recall the relations.** For the hydrogen atom,
K = **−E** ✓
U = **2E** ✓
and indeed K + U = −E + 2E = E ✓ consistent.
**Step 2 — substitute E = −3·4 eV.**
K = **+3·4 eV** ✓
U = **−6·8 eV** ✓
**Step 3 — check the sum.**
3·4 + (−6·8) = **−3·4 eV** ✓ the given total.
**Why the kinetic energy is positive.** It is ½mv², which can never be negative ✓ The
electron is always moving.
**Why the potential energy is negative.** The zero is taken at **infinite
separation** ✓ A bound electron sits in the Coulomb well, below that reference.
**The virial theorem.** For any inverse-square force,
**2⟨K⟩ = −⟨U⟩** ✓
so the kinetic energy is always **half** the magnitude of the potential. Here
2(3·4) = 6·8 ✓ The same theorem governs planetary orbits and star clusters.
**Which level this is.** E_n = −13·6/n² = −3·4 gives n² = 4, so **n = 2** ✓ the first
excited state.
**The other quantities at n = 2.**
radius: 4 x 0·529 = **2·12 Å** ✓
speed: 2·18 x 10⁶/2 = **1·09 x 10⁶ m s⁻¹** ✓
and a check: ½mv² = ½(9·1 x 10⁻³¹)(1·19 x 10¹²) = 5·4 x 10⁻¹⁹ J = **3·4 eV** ✓
**The ionisation energy from this level.** **3·4 eV** ✓ exactly the magnitude of the
total energy - the work needed to carry the electron to infinity and leave it at rest.
**Why the total energy is negative for any bound state.** Binding means the system
cannot fly apart without an input of energy ✓ A **positive** total energy would
describe a free electron passing by on a hyperbolic path.
**How the three scale with n.**
E ∝ **−1/n²**, K ∝ **1/n²**, U ∝ **−1/n²** ✓
All three shrink in magnitude as the electron moves outward, approaching zero at
n = ∞.
**Reading the distractors.** **K = −3·4 eV** ✗ is impossible - kinetic energy cannot be
negative. **K = −6·8, U = +3·4** ✗ reverses both signs, and **K = 10·2, U = −13·6** ✗
would give a total of −3·4 but violates the virial theorem ✓
∴ K = 3.4 eV, U = − 6.8 eV.

Bohr quantises angular momentum as **nh/2π**, so the change is **3h/2π**.
**Step 1 — state the quantisation condition.**
L_n = **nh/2π = nℏ** ✓
**Step 2 — write the two values.**
L₄ = **4h/2π** ✓
L₁ = **1h/2π** ✓
**Step 3 — take the difference.**
ΔL = (4 − 1)h/2π
= **3h/2π** ✓
**Why the change is a whole number of ℏ.** Angular momentum comes in **integer
multiples** of ℏ in the Bohr model ✓ so any transition changes it by an integer number
of these units - here three.
**Where the quantisation came from.** Bohr simply **postulated** it in 1913 ✓ Its
justification came a decade later from **de Broglie**: the allowed orbits are those
whose circumference holds a whole number of electron wavelengths,
2πr = nλ with λ = h/mv ✓
which rearranges at once to mvr = nh/2π.
**The energy released in this jump.**
E₄ − E₁ = −0·85 − (−13·6) = **12·75 eV** ✓
giving a photon of λ = 1240/12·75 = **97·2 nm** - the third line of the **Lyman**
series, in the far ultraviolet.
**Where the angular momentum goes.** The emitted **photon** carries it away ✓ A photon
has spin ℏ, so strictly a single photon cannot remove 3ℏ - the transition proceeds
either through intermediate levels or, rarely, by multi-photon emission. The Bohr model
does not address this subtlety.
**The other quantities that change.**
radius: from 16a₀ to a₀, a factor of **16** ✓
speed: from v₁/4 to v₁, a factor of **4** ✓
energy: from −0·85 to **−13·6 eV** ✓
**The value of ℏ.**
ℏ = h/2π = **1·055 x 10⁻³⁴ J s** ✓ so ΔL = 3ℏ = 3·16 x 10⁻³⁴ J s - utterly minute,
which is why quantisation is invisible in everyday rotation.
**Why the selection rule matters in the full theory.** Quantum mechanics requires
Δl = ±1 for a single-photon transition ✓ The Bohr model, lacking the quantum number l,
cannot express this - another sign that it is a stepping stone rather than the final
account.
**Reading the distractors.** **h/2π** ✗ and **2h/2π** ✗ correspond to changes of 1 and
2 in n. **4h/2π** ✗ is the **initial** value, not the change ✓
∴ 3h/2π.

Five days is **half** a half-life, so the survival factor is **2^(−1/2)**.
**Step 1 — write the decay law.**
N = N₀(½)^(t/T) ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.** With t = 5 days and T = 10 days:
N = 1000x (½)^(0·5) ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
(½)^(0·5) = 1/√2 = **0·707** ✓
N = 1000x x 0·707
= **707x** ✓
**Why it is not 500x.** Decay is **exponential**, not linear ✓ Half the time does
**not** mean half the decay. The survivors after 5 days are 70·7%, not 50% - and 500x
is the designed trap.
**The sequence over successive five-day intervals.**
0 days: **1000x** ✓
5 days: **707x** ✓
10 days: **500x** ✓ one half-life
15 days: **354x**
20 days: **250x** ✓ two half-lives
Each five-day step multiplies by the same factor 0·707 - the hallmark of an
exponential.
**Why 1/√2 appears.** Because 5 days is **half** a half-life ✓
(½)^(1/2) = 1/√2 = **0·707**, the square root of the halving factor.
**The decay constant.**
λ = 0·693/10 = **0·0693 per day** ✓
and a check: N = 1000x e^(−0·0693 x 5) = 1000x e^(−0·347) = **707x** ✓
**The number that have decayed.**
1000x − 707x = **293x** ✓ not 500x, which again underlines that the process is not
linear in time.
**Why the decay is exponential.** Every surviving nucleus has the **same** probability
of decaying in the next instant, regardless of its age ✓ A constant hazard rate
produces dN/dt = −λN, whose solution is the exponential.
**The memoryless property.** A nucleus does not **age** ✓ After 5 days the 707x
survivors are statistically identical to a fresh sample of 707x nuclei - which is why
the next five days remove the same **fraction**, not the same number.
**Reading the distractors.** **500x** ✗ assumes linear decay. **750x** ✗ is a rough
linear interpolation, and **250x** ✗ is the figure after **two** half-lives ✓
∴ 707 x.

The recoil energy is **E²/(2Mc²)** - the photon's momentum shared with a heavy
nucleus.
**Step 1 — conserve momentum.** The nucleus was at rest, so it recoils with the
photon's momentum:
p = **E/c** ✓
**Step 2 — write the recoil kinetic energy.** The nucleus is non-relativistic:
K = p²/(2M)
= **E²/(2Mc²)** ✓
**Step 3 — find Mc² for the nucleus.**
M = 20 x 1·6 x 10⁻²⁷ = **3·2 x 10⁻²⁶ kg**
Mc² = (3·2 x 10⁻²⁶)(9 x 10¹⁶) = 2·88 x 10⁻⁹ J ✓
in electron volts: 2·88 x 10⁻⁹/1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ = **1·8 x 10¹⁰ eV = 18000 MeV** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
K = (6)²/(2 x 18000) MeV
= 36/36000
= 10⁻³ MeV
= **1 keV** ✓
**Why the recoil is so small.** The nucleus is **enormously** heavier than the photon's
equivalent mass ✓ The fraction of the energy it takes is
E/(2Mc²) = 6/36000 = **1/6000** ✓ so 5999 parts in 6000 go to the photon.
**Why the recoil matters at all.** It means the emitted photon's energy is **slightly
less** than the nuclear transition energy ✓ and an identical nucleus cannot resonantly
absorb it, since it would need the extra keV for its own recoil. The emission and
absorption lines are shifted apart by **2 keV**.
**The Mossbauer effect.** Embed the nucleus in a **crystal lattice** and the recoil is
taken up by the **whole crystal**, of effectively infinite mass ✓ Then K → 0, the
photon carries the full transition energy, and resonant absorption becomes possible.
Mossbauer won the Nobel Prize in 1961 for this.
**Why it is so precise a tool.** Recoil-free gamma lines have a relative width of about
**10⁻¹³** ✓ sharp enough to measure the gravitational redshift over 22 m in the
Pound-Rebka experiment.
**The nucleus's recoil speed.**
v = p/M = (E/c)/M = 6 x 10⁶ x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹/(3 x 10⁸ x 3·2 x 10⁻²⁶) = **10⁵ m s⁻¹** ✓
fast by everyday standards, but carrying only a keV because the mass is so small.
**Reading the distractors.** **10 keV**, **0·1 keV** and **100 keV** ✗ differ by powers
of ten ✓ The arithmetic E²/(2Mc²) = 36/36000 MeV fixes it at exactly 1 keV.
∴ 1 KeV.

A d.c. supply needs **rectification**, then **smoothing**, then **regulation** - in
that order.
**Step 1 — rectify.** The alternating input must first be converted to a
**unidirectional** output ✓ A bridge of four diodes gives full-wave rectification, but
the result is a **pulsating** d.c. - a series of humps, not a steady voltage.
**Step 2 — filter.** A large capacitor charges at each peak and discharges slowly
between them ✓ smoothing the humps into a nearly steady voltage with a small
**ripple**.
**Step 3 — regulate.** A Zener diode or an integrated regulator holds the output
**constant** despite variations in the input or the load ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** **Rectifier, filter, regulator** ✓
**Why the order cannot be changed.** Each stage needs the previous one's output ✓
A filter before the rectifier would merely smooth an **alternating** wave, leaving it
alternating. A regulator before the rectifier would have nothing steady to work with.
**What each stage removes.**
rectifier: the **negative** half-cycles ✓
filter: the **ripple** ✓
regulator: the remaining **variation** with input and load ✓
**Why the question says "variable AC".** A regulator is essential precisely because
the input is not steady ✓ A fixed mains voltage and a constant load would need only
the first two stages.
**The ripple factor.** For a full-wave rectifier with a capacitor filter,
r ≈ **1/(4√3 fRC)** ✓ so a larger capacitor or a lighter load gives smoother output -
which is why power supplies carry such large electrolytic capacitors.
**How a Zener regulates.** Operated in **reverse breakdown**, it holds a nearly
constant voltage across itself ✓ while a series resistor absorbs the surplus. More
sophisticated regulators use a transistor pass element with feedback.
**A modern alternative.** A **switched-mode** supply chops the rectified d.c. at high
frequency, transforms it with a small core, and rectifies again ✓ far more efficient
and lighter, but the same three functions are present in a different arrangement.
**Why full-wave is preferred to half-wave.** Twice the ripple frequency and twice the
average output ✓ making the filter's job far easier.
**Reading the distractors.** Every other order places a stage before the one that must
feed it ✓ The sequence is forced by the physics.
∴ Rectifier, filter, regulator.

The length goes as **T²**, so find each period and square the ratio.
**Step 1 — find each period.**
A: 10 oscillations in 20 s, so T_A = **2 s** ✓
B: 8 oscillations in 10 s, so T_B = 10/8 = **1·25 s** ✓
**Step 2 — recall the pendulum formula.**
T = 2π√(l/g), so **l ∝ T²** ✓
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
l_A/l_B = (T_A/T_B)²
= (2/1·25)²
= (1·6)² ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
= 2·56
= **64/25** ✓
**Why the square.** The period depends on the **square root** of the length ✓ so the
length depends on the **square** of the period. A pendulum twice as long swings only
√2 = 1·41 times as slowly.
**The actual lengths, with g = 9·8.**
A: l = gT²/4π² = 9·8(4)/39·48 = **0·993 m** ✓ the familiar "seconds pendulum" of
about a metre
B: 9·8(1·5625)/39·48 = **0·388 m** ✓
and 0·993/0·388 = **2·56** ✓
**Why the mass of the bob is irrelevant.** It cancels from the equation of motion ✓
Just as all bodies fall at the same rate, all bobs on the same string swing with the
same period.
**Why the amplitude is irrelevant - almost.** For **small** oscillations the period is
independent of amplitude ✓ which is what makes a pendulum a clock. At 30° the period is
already 1·7% longer, which is why pendulum clocks use small swings.
**How a pendulum measures g.** Rearranging,
g = **4π²l/T²** ✓ Timing many oscillations gives T very precisely, and l is easily
measured - the classic school determination of g.
**Why "10 oscillations in 20 seconds" rather than one.** Timing many swings and
dividing reduces the **fractional error** in T ✓ and since g depends on T², that error
counts **twice** over.
**A quick mental check.** A is the **slower** pendulum, so it must be the **longer** ✓
and the ratio must exceed 1 - which rules out 25/64 at once.
**Reading the distractors.** **25/64** ✗ inverts the ratio. **8/5** ✗ and **5/4** ✗ are
the ratios of the **periods** or of the oscillation counts, with the squaring forgotten ✓
∴ 64/25.

Sound in a pipe is **longitudinal**, and reflection at the ends makes it
**stationary**.
**Step 1 — why longitudinal.** Sound in a **gas** propagates by compressions and
rarefactions **along** the direction of travel ✓ A gas has **no modulus of rigidity**,
so it cannot sustain the shear a transverse wave would require.
**Step 2 — why stationary.** The wave reflects from the **closed** end and from the
open end too ✓ The incident and reflected waves, of equal frequency and amplitude,
superpose to form a **standing** wave with fixed nodes and antinodes.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Longitudinal and stationary** ✓
**The pattern in a closed pipe.**
a **node** at the **closed** end - the air cannot move there ✓
an **antinode** at the **open** end - the air is free to oscillate ✓
so the shortest pipe holds a **quarter** wavelength.
**The harmonics.**
fundamental: **f = v/4L** ✓
then **3f, 5f, 7f** … - only the **odd** harmonics ✓
which is why a closed pipe sounds an octave below an open pipe of the same length, and
why it has a distinctive, hollow tone.
**The contrast with an open pipe.** Antinodes at **both** ends, a half wavelength in
the shortest case, and **all** harmonics present ✓ f = v/2L.
**Why a stationary wave transports no energy.** The two travelling waves carry equal
energy in **opposite** directions ✓ so the net flow is zero. Energy merely sloshes back
and forth between kinetic and potential forms.
**Where the pressure and displacement sit.** They are **out of step** ✓ A displacement
**node** is a pressure **antinode** and vice versa - which is why a microphone placed
at the closed end, where the air does not move, registers the **largest** pressure
swing.
**Why sound cannot be transverse in air.** A transverse wave needs the medium to resist
**shear** ✓ Gases and liquids have no rigidity modulus, which is also why **S waves**
from earthquakes cannot cross the Earth's liquid outer core.
**Where the musical instruments stand.** The clarinet behaves as a **closed** pipe -
odd harmonics only, hence its distinctive timbre ✓ The flute behaves as an **open**
pipe, with all harmonics.
**Reading the distractors.** Both **transverse** options ✗ are impossible in a gas.
**Longitudinal and progressive** ✗ would describe sound travelling freely in the open,
not confined between reflecting ends ✓
∴ Longitudinal and Stationary.
